stem: For two scalar input features and a scalar output, what geometric object does ordinary affine linear regression fit in the joint input-output space?

options.text: One plane giving a scalar height above each two-feature input location
One straight line containing all input-output triples in three dimensions
Two separate straight-line predictions, with no single output defined for a pair of inputs
A generally curved surface whose slope in one input automatically varies with the other

citations.locator: Printed slide 6: right-hand Algorithm goal list, underlined “Two features: A plane.”

stem: Suppose the fitted model has b₀=−14.7 N·m, b₁=9.511764705882353 N·m/kg and b₂=15.56470588235294 N. What torque does it predict at m=3.5 kg and r=0.8 m, rounded to two decimals?
assumptions: Coefficients are supplied from an ordinary least-squares fit with intercept to the four printed examples; input order remains mass then extension.

stem: The source’s four labels follow the supplied physical product τ=9.8mr. Why need an affine fit in raw features (m,r) differ from that product at a new point?

options.text: The product contains a mass-distance interaction absent from b₀+b₁m+b₂r
The free intercept supplies the interaction because it shifts the plane for each input pair
The slope b₁ in a raw-feature affine fit is recomputed as 9.8r at every prediction point
The separate terms b₁m and b₂r are multiplied together when the fitted model predicts

assumptions: Compare the printed raw-feature affine model with the explicitly supplied static point-load product, not a claim that all robot torque obeys that simple product.

stem: A model with too few informative features has high training and high test error. What change directly addresses the stated underfitting cause?

options.text: Repeat the already converged optimization longer without changing inputs or model family
Change only the train-test split while keeping the same incomplete inputs and fitted model family
Add measurements of relevant informative features that are currently missing from the inputs
Collect more samples of the same incomplete features while leaving the missing information unmeasured

assumptions: Optimization has converged for the current model; the question stipulates insufficient informative features as the cause, not merely infers it from error rates.

citations.locator: Printed slide 9: right-hand Underfitting column, high training/test error and Causes: Insufficient features.

stem: How should the slide’s “too many training iterations” overfitting cause be used responsibly?

options.text: Choose the stopping point at the lowest training error, using continued training improvement as sufficient evidence of generalization
Transfer the best epoch count from one model and dataset to another without rechecking held-out performance
Diagnose overfitting from a high iteration count alone, even when both training and held-out errors are still improving
Treat it as a possible risk in an iterative training setup, using held-out performance to judge when further fitting hurts generalization

citations.locator: Printed slide 9: left-hand Overfitting Causes line including too many training iterations.

stem: Which conclusion respects what temperature/Wi-Fi clustering can establish about physical rooms?

options.text: A change of cluster label along a route establishes that the robot crossed a physical room boundary
Two adjoining rooms must receive different cluster labels even when their sensor readings overlap
A feature cluster can contain spatially separated locations whose temperature and Wi-Fi readings are similar
A feature cluster must be spatially connected because Euclidean distances are used between its sensor readings

citations.locator: Printed slide 14: Data Architecture lists only temperature and Wi-Fi inputs, no labeled output data; motivation asks for three zones.

stem: The slide writes temperature 10±2 and Wi-Fi 20±5 for the Gaussian example. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: The plus/minus values ensure Wi-Fi can never exceed 100% in any generated zone
These describe mean and standard deviation, not guaranteed minimum and maximum values
Every temperature lies in [8,12] and every Wi-Fi value in [15,25]
The first number is always a variance and the second is a mean

citations.locator: Printed slide 15: np.random.normal location and scale arrays plus the standard-deviation annotation
Printed slide 17: upper sensor cluster in the scatter plot; purple observation markers above the 100% horizontal Wi-Fi gridline

stem: Suppose a second implementation produces identical groups but relabels the source’s cluster 0 as cluster 2. Does that alone mean the clustering is worse?

options.text: No; a consistent permutation of cluster IDs leaves the partition unchanged
Yes; label 0 always means the highest-quality cluster
Yes; cluster number must equal the zone_A/B/C generation order
No; labels can be changed independently for individual points without changing the partition

citations.locator: Printed slide 17: scatter plot labels Zone 0, Zone 1 and Zone 2 around the three sensor groups, and marks the new reading in Zone 0.

stem: An unsupervised monitor flags a joint-torque pattern as unusual. What is the most defensible interpretation of the lecture’s mechanical-failure example?

options.text: It identifies mechanical failure rather than changed operating conditions because the detector used torque data
It identifies a sensor fault rather than a mechanical fault because the monitor did not use failure labels
It identifies harmless distribution shift rather than failure whenever the flagged pattern was absent from training
It may indicate a problem requiring investigation, but an anomaly alone does not identify its cause

citations.locator: Printed slide 18: Unsupervised Task/Robotics Application table, Anomaly detection row about abnormal joint-torque patterns and mechanical failure.

stem: How does grouping similar pixel colors support the image-compression example?

options.text: Replace each color by its cluster center while requiring every original color to remain exactly recoverable
Replace similar original colors by a smaller palette of representative colors, accepting possible reconstruction error
Store a cluster ID in addition to every unchanged full-precision pixel color, treating the extra labels as the compression
Retain one distinct palette entry for every original color, using clustering only to reorder those entries

assumptions: Interpret the slide’s color-grouping mechanism as palette reduction; net file size also depends on palette and index encoding overhead.

citations.locator: Printed slide 18: Unsupervised Task/Robotics Application table, Image Compression row about similar pixel colors and fewer bits.

stem: A navigation controller can choose {left, right, forward} and now chooses left. Which terminology distinguishes the set from the selected move?

options.text: {left, right, forward} is the action set; left is the new observed state rather than a selected move
{left, right, forward} is one selected action; left is the entire action set
{left, right, forward} is the state space; left is a policy mapping observations to decisions
{left, right, forward} is the action set; left is the selected action

citations.locator: Printed slide 19: Core Elements, Action(a) definition as a set of possible moves.

stem: The slide describes rewards as arriving only after a sequence of actions, while the next slide shows action then reward in a repeated loop. Which qualified statement accommodates both examples?

options.text: A reward after a single action cannot be used in reinforcement learning
Every RL task must reveal the correct action as a supervised label
Only the final action can influence a delayed reward
Rewards may be immediate or delayed; delayed consequences create a credit-assignment challenge

citations.locator: Printed slide 19: learning-with-a-critic bullet, rewards or penalties only after a sequence of actions.
Printed slide 20: reinforcement-learning loop arrows, 2 Takes ACTION → 3 Environment gives REWARD → 4 Robot updates its Brain → repeat.

stem: A controller interacts with a simulated navigation world rather than hardware. Is that excluded by the agent/environment interaction idea?

options.text: No; a fixed log of one route provides the same interactive responses for any alternative action the agent chooses
Yes; an environment must contain the policy that chooses the agent’s action, rather than respond to that action
No; a simulator can provide action-dependent state transitions and reward feedback, fulfilling the functional environment role
Yes; simulator feedback cannot serve as reinforcement feedback until a physical robot repeats the same actions

assumptions: The supplied simulator responds to the agent’s selected actions and provides observations and reward feedback; no claim is made that it perfectly represents hardware.

citations.locator: Printed slide 19: Environment definition with parenthetical physical world, alongside trial-and-error agent/environment interaction.
